Marks the cell visited in place

p: Grid rows `11000 / 11000 / 00100 / 00011`. Each time the scan finds a `1`, it counts one island and sinks all its cells.

blocks.h: Why does sinking replace a visited set?
p: Once a land cell becomes `'0'`, the outer loop will never start from it and the DFS will never re-enter it, which is exactly what a visited set provides. The cost is that the input grid is destroyed; if the caller needs it back, copy it first or use a separate `seen` set (O(m·n) extra space).

A single huge island makes the recursion as deep as the island size (up to m·n). Python's default limit (~1000) breaks on a 100×100 all-land grid; use an explicit stack or BFS with a deque for large grids.

bullets: Time: O(m·n), every cell is visited a constant number of times.

200.takeaway: Count connected components on a grid: scan, and on each unvisited land cell run a DFS/BFS that marks the whole island, adding 1 per start.

One new large element can make several left elements removable at once, and the window should shrink as far as it can while still reaching the target. `if` would remove only one element and miss shorter windows.

p: Shrinking from the left always lowers the sum and growing always raises it only if values are positive. With negatives, a bigger window could have a smaller sum and the greedy shrink would skip valid answers; you would need a monotonic deque over prefix sums (problem 862).

209.takeaway: Smallest subarray with sum ≥ target in positives: expand right, shrink left while valid — a two-pointer sliding window.

p: We want to throw away the smallest of the current k+1 candidates. A min-heap gives the smallest in O(1) and removes it in O(log k). After the whole array is processed, the smallest of the survivors (`heap[0]`) is exactly the kth largest.
Heap is the safe interview answer: predictable O(n log k) and works on streams. Quickselect has better average time but a bad worst case unless pivots are randomised.

215.takeaway: Kth largest: keep a min-heap of size k; its top is the answer. Quickselect is the O(n) average alternative.

p: `"3+2*2"` — each row is the moment a number ends and its pending operator is applied.

`*` and `/` bind tighter than `+` and `-`. By pushing additive terms and combining multiplicative ones straight into the top of the stack, `3+2*2` becomes stack `[3, 4]` and the sum is 7. No second pass or parentheses handling is needed.
For negative results `//` floors: `-7 // 2 = -4`, but the problem wants truncation toward zero: `int(-7 / 2) = -3`. (Floating division is exact enough for LeetCode's 32-bit range.)

bullets: Space: O(n) for the stack (O(1) possible by tracking only the last term).

227.takeaway: Precedence without parsing trees: defer + and - by pushing signed terms, apply * and / immediately to the top term, sum at the end.

blocks.h: Why can a single return value mean two things?
p: If one target is an ancestor of the other, the first one found is returned all the way up: the search never reaches the descendant, but that is fine because the ancestor is the LCA by definition (a node may be its own descendant). Both `p` and `q` exist in the tree. If one may be missing, you would need to count how many targets were found (that is problem 1644).

bullets: Time: O(n), visits each node once.

236.takeaway: LCA of a binary tree: post-order recursion returning a target or the LCA; the first node where both sides are non-null is the answer.

blocks.h: Why store indices and not values?
p: We need to know when the front element leaves the window. Indices carry both the value (`nums[i]`) and the position needed for the expiry test. Values alone cannot tell you whether an element is still in the window. (In this example nothing expires, but with `[5, 1, 1, 1]` and `k = 3` the index 0 reaches the front and leaves the window at `i = 3`, because `0 <= 3 - 3`.)

blocks.h: Why is each element O(1) amortised?
p: Every index is appended once and removed once (from the back when dominated, or from the front when expired). So the total number of operations is at most 2n.
The `<=` in the pop condition drops equal values. Keeping only the newest of equals is safe because it stays in the window longer. A strict `<` would also be correct but keep unnecessary duplicates.

bullets: Space: O(k) for the deque, plus the output.

239.takeaway: Sliding window maximum: keep a monotonic decreasing deque of indices; the front is the max, pop dominated elements from the back, expire from the front.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Find ways to split the remaining value `n` into factors that are all ≥ `start`; `path` holds the factors chosen so far
Backtracking where the remaining target shrinks
Try factors `f` from `start` up to √n; `isqrt` is the exact integer square root
If `f > √n`, then `n // f < f`, which would repeat an earlier order
Emit the pair as a complete factorisation (the two last factors)
Keep factoring the cofactor, with `start = f` so factors never decrease

p: `n = 12`: each divisor `f` from 2 to 3 (√12 ≈ 3.46) produces one emitted combination and then recurses on `n // f`.

blocks.h: Why `start = f` in the recursive call?
p: Keeping factors in non-decreasing order makes every multiset appear exactly once (`2·2·3`, never also `2·3·2` or `3·2·2`). It also lets the loop stop at √n: once `f*f > n` the cofactor `n // f` would be smaller than `f`, which breaks the order.

blocks.h: Why not recurse for the last pair?
p: The pair `[f, n // f]` is emitted directly as the final two factors; recursing on `n // f` then handles splitting that cofactor further (as in `[2, 2, 3]`). The number 1 and `n` itself are never used as factors.

bullets: Time: exponential in the number of prime factors; each output is built in O(length). There is no tight closed form; it is bounded by the number of factorisations times their length.
Space: O(log n) recursion depth (factors are ≥ 2), plus the output.

254.takeaway: Factor combinations: backtrack on non-decreasing factors up to √n, emitting `path + [f, n//f]` and recursing on the cofactor.

p: `nums = [1,2,1,3,2,5]`. The XOR of everything is `3 ^ 5 = 6` (`110`), so the lowest differing bit is `010`. Splitting by it:
Numbers with the bit set: XOR of [2, 3, 2] = 3. Then the other number is `6 ^ 3 = 5`. The answer is `[3, 5]`.

blocks.h: Why does splitting by a differing bit work?
p: `a` and `b` are different, so `a ^ b` has at least one 1-bit; at that bit one of them has 0 and the other 1, so they fall into different groups. Each duplicate pair has identical numbers, so both land in the same group and cancel. Each group therefore holds exactly one unique number.
